title: Order matters
prompt: For FizzBuzz (multiples of 3 → "Fizz", of 5 → "Buzz", of both → "FizzBuzz"), why must `n % 15 == 0` be checked first?
options: Because `n % 3 == 0` is also true for 15, so checking it first would print "Fizz" and never reach the FizzBuzz case
It doesn't matter — any order works
explanation: if/else chains stop at the FIRST true branch. When conditions overlap, put the most specific one first.

title: Ternary syntax
code:
int max = a > b {{1}} a {{2}} b;
String sign = x >= 0 ? {{3}} : "negative";
explanation: condition `?` whenTrue `:` whenFalse. Both branches must produce a value of the same type.

title: Fall-through
prompt:
With `x = 1`, what does this print?
`switch (x) { case 1: System.out.println("one"); case 2: System.out.println("two"); break; default: System.out.println("other"); }`
options: `one` then `two` — case 1 has no break, so it falls through into case 2
explanation: Without `break`, execution continues into the next case's code. The `break` in case 2 stops it before `default`.

title: FizzBuzz (single value)
prompt: Return `"FizzBuzz"` if `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5, `"Fizz"` if only by 3, `"Buzz"` if only by 5, otherwise the number itself as a string (`String.valueOf(n)`).

solution.explanation: Most specific condition first. `return` exits immediately, so no `else` is needed — a very common clean-code style.

hints: Divisible by both 3 and 5 means divisible by 15.
`String.valueOf(n)` converts an int to a String.
